A user said one CLI command puts all your auth data in your own DB, with no lock-in to a DB provider. They use the built-in OAuth providers for Google, Apple and GitHub logins. Unlike Supabase or Clerk, it costs $0.
One commenter tried Better Auth last year, still found it lacking, and noted it seemed to be run by one guy.
A developer integrating it into a new product: "it is absolutely fantastic. It just works."

A developer building auth for a user app, client dashboards and internal tools gets all of this from included plugins and defaults, without writing a single line of special code: anonymous users upgradable to real users, organizations, multi-tenancy and many sign-in options. "It just works and I own all the data."
A team found it far more hackable than Clerk. They added a plugin enabling auth via iframe postMessage (embedded in a CRM), and everything worked seamlessly.
A user recalled its "request header based" design. Running admin scripts and tests was very hacky, because if you skipped that, plugins wouldn't run.

One commenter noted Better Auth supports email/password out of the box. By contrast, NextAuth has a preachy disclaimer and leaves you to implement password hashing yourself. Better Auth feels more developer-focused.

A consultant builds client MVPs with Better Auth. They prefer it for flexibility: adding a user field is just a new Postgres column, versus appending data through Cognito/Auth0/Okta APIs in a rigid format.
A user running it in production apps called it the best open-source option for TypeScript developers implementing auth, and said it is documented very well.
"better-auth is a joy to use. great dx with the type-safe plugin system... the quality of the lib and the docs is really high."
A team found it immediately better than existing TypeScript auth libraries, with no Next.js lock-in. They migrated from Next.js to Hono and only had to change the router.

A user reported a security vulnerability. Within 24 hours it was patched, a notice was posted, and they were credited with a CVE. They also found the library more flexible and easier to understand than others.

A user migrated from Lucia and said it just works, with some quirks. The auth client handles everything instead of giving you server-side helper functions for customizing login/register, so they had to restructure login error handling. The CLI-generated migration made switching easy.

Compared to Lucia's full control, they like Better Auth's built-in email verification, password resets and rate limiting. Those were features they dreaded coding; here they are built in or simple plugins.
A user loved better-auth's DX but worries about Vercel adding reliance on its closed cloud. They noted the database adapter design makes it relatively easy to switch to another provider or library.
"Better auth is an absolute dumpster fire codebase."
A commenter said it does far more than next-auth/auth.js: authn/z, acting as an identity provider and OIDC/SSO provider, RBAC, and SAML/SCIM. Some of those features are enterprise-only.

Adding passkeys with better-auth took about 7 lines of server code and virtually no client API change, versus Microsoft's lengthy .NET Core guide. "For ease-of-use and development speed, better-auth has been a clear winner for me."
"This framework has made auth such a non-issue for me. The setup is easy and the usage is consistent framework to framework."
A user wanted to use Better Auth in an iOS app, but the client library is JS-only. There is virtually no documentation on writing your own client library.
